Decision — non-root install, per-service users, mesh-first ports

Status: proposed 2026-10-12. Builds on one repository, install profiles and the one-system-binary design (every headless daemon a personality of mix, chosen by argv[0]), which needs its own decision record.

The question

The server programs (maild, webd, dnsd and the rest) are moving into MixOS, headed for one mix binary. Updates already reach desktop users through releasesd, which by rule never changes anything as root. Can a whole node, servers included, be installed and kept current without root, and how do unprivileged daemons serve ports 25, 53, 443, 465, 587 and 993?

Where these servers run

The usual MixOS server is a node on its owner's own WireGuard mesh, a /24 of their machines. Mail, web and DNS are served to that mesh, not to the internet. A server that must take connections from outside the mesh (an MX on public port 25, a public website on 443) is the exception. This record covers the mesh case and states what it does not settle for the public one.

The decision

1. Root installs once; updates never need it

  • Bootstrap (root, once per node, and again only when units change): create the system users, install the unit, socket, sysusers and tmpfiles files, and hand the server prefix to the mixos user.
  • The server prefix /opt/mixos is owned by the system user mixos. A releasesd instance running as mixos keeps it current, with the same checks as a desktop install (GitHub digest and SHA256SUMS, staged unpack, previous version kept for rollback). It uses releasesd's existing layout through its environment: MIXOS_RELEASES_ROOT=/opt/mixos, so releases land in /opt/mixos/opt/<app>/<version> and their programs are linked into /opt/mixos/bin. The unit paths (/opt/mixos/bin/<daemon>) do not change.
  • Desktop installs stay per user in ~/.local, as today.
  • Binaries are readable and executable by everyone and writable only by mixos. No daemon runs as mixos.

2. Every daemon runs as its own user

  • Each server daemon runs as its own system user (maild, webd, dnsd and so on), declared in its component's sysusers fragment. Never as root, never as a login user, never as mixos.
  • Each daemon's state lives in its own StateDirectory=, which no other service user can read. A compromised webd cannot read mail, keys or the login user's home.
  • Units use systemd's sandboxing (NoNewPrivileges=yes, ProtectSystem=strict, ProtectHome=yes, PrivateTmp=yes and a CapabilityBoundingSet= that names only what the daemon needs), and each component's units are reviewed against that list.

3. Privileged ports come from systemd

  • Socket activation is the target. A system .socket unit binds the privileged ports as root and passes the open sockets to the daemon (LISTEN_FDS). The daemon never holds a capability. Socket activation also keeps the listening socket open across a restart, so an upgrade drops no connections that are still queued.
  • Interim: a daemon that cannot take inherited sockets yet gets AmbientCapabilities=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE with CapabilityBoundingSet=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE in its unit. Taking inherited sockets is part of each port's definition of done (maild, webd, dnsd).
  • Not file capabilities. The kernel clears them whenever the file is replaced, so every update would silently lose the ports. In the one binary they would also give the mix shell, and every script, the right to bind 443.
  • Not lowering net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start by default. It applies to every user on the node. A node owner may still choose it for a single-user machine, but MixOS does not do it for them.

4. Mesh first

  • Server daemons listen on the node's mesh address by default, never on every address. The .socket units name the mesh address (ListenStream=<mesh-ip>:25, with FreeBind=yes so the socket can be bound before the WireGuard interface is up).
  • Listening on a public address is an explicit per-node configuration, never a default and never part of an install profile.

5. Applying an update without root

  • releasesd (as mixos) moves current and records the transition in meta.json. A root-owned systemd .path unit watches that file and starts a root service that restarts only the units whose component version or hash changed in the release manifest. The mixos user triggers the restart but never controls which units restart or how.
  • A release whose units, sysusers or tmpfiles fragments changed cannot be applied by mixos. releasesd installs the binaries, reports that the bootstrap step is needed, and leaves the running services on the previous version until a root user runs the installer.

6. What still needs root at run time

  • nspawnd: systemd-nspawn needs root. It stays a root service in its own profile, outside this model.
  • noded: reading network state needs nothing; changing it needs CAP_NET_ADMIN, granted in its unit the same way as the interim port capability, only if that node uses the feature.
  • compd: none. Seat, input and display access come through logind and libseat, as today.

Not settled: servers open to the internet

A daemon that accepts connections from outside the mesh (an MX on public port 25, a public website on 443) faces hostile traffic. Running it as its own sandboxed user, with the port granted by systemd, is still the baseline. It is not shown to be enough: rate limits, DoS behaviour, TLS and ACME exposure, whether the public listener should be its own process or node, and firewall policy all belong to a separate decision before any public listener ships as a supported configuration.

Why

  • Updates without root are what make the releasesd model work for a whole operating system: no package manager, no distribution repository, and no root shell for routine updates.
  • Per-service users limit what one compromised daemon can reach. Running every daemon as the login user would have been simpler, but would have handed a mail-server bug the owner's SSH keys and secrets.
  • Ports from systemd grant the right per service and per port, survive updates, and keep capabilities away from the shell that shares the binary.
  • Mesh first matches how MixOS servers are used, and keeps the internet-facing case visible as the exception it is.

Alternatives

  • Everything as the login user (user units with lingering, plus the sysctl). Rejected: no isolation between daemons or from the owner's home.
  • File capabilities on mix. Rejected: lost on every update, and granted to every script.
  • Root installs through a package manager. Rejected: it is the dependency that releasesd removes.
  • Root-run releasesd for the server prefix. Rejected: releasesd's trust rule (never act as root) is what makes a bad release unable to take over the node. A fixed .path unit for restarts keeps root's part small.

Consequences

  • Each server component ships a sysusers fragment, its units with the sandboxing list, and .socket units for its ports. The install-profile resolver lists them, as that decision already requires.
  • maild, webd and dnsd learn to take inherited sockets as part of their ports.
  • releasesd gains a server instance (mixos user, /opt/mixos root) and a "units changed" result. The restart service and its .path unit are new work, alongside the installer the install-profiles decision calls for.
  • The bootstrap installer is the only routine root step, and it runs again only when a release changes units.
